text:
maria: Quick heads-up — during the 4k-token stress sims the KV cache memory climbs steadily (~10% over 30s) instead of plateauing. Not a single huge allocation, more like slow accumulation.
kevin: Ugh. Can you paste the perf traces / pprof?
maria: Pasted a small snippet from the heap profile: 
```
# heap profile (top)
bytes  objects  stack
1.2MB  12000    kv::block::Small(32) allocator
800KB  4000     kv::block::Medium(256) allocator
300KB  40       kv::longcontext entries (pin)
...
```
kevin: Small-blocks are the bulk. Is allocator splitting into many 32B chunks? That smells like slab fragmentation after repeated small allocations.
ashley: Also check the eviction/sample skew. If batching keeps old contexts pinned, we won't free their KV and the free pool gets fragmented. Any correlation with batching changes in the last rollout?
maria: We did roll a batching tweak last week that increases batch depth for low-latency paths (dev rollout id 2026-03-09). I ran a quick diff and saw more interleaved long-context requests.
samir: Hypothesis: increased batch depth -> more interleaving -> longer-lived KV entries across many small allocations -> fragmentation of small-slab. Two approaches: tune block size mix or compact occasionally.
nisha: For compaction: we discussed low-cost in-place compactor earlier. If we can do incremental compaction (background, bounded CPU) and target buckets with high free-fragment ratio, should help. But need eviction policy changes so we don't thrash.
maria: I tried a naive compact pass that walks small-bucket freelist and coalesces if adjacent. Latency impact ~2–5ms per pass on a 16GB node, CPU ~0.4 core. Results: mem drop ~6% for the run.
kevin: Not bad for a stopgap. What about tuning allocator: larger minimum block (64B) to reduce metadata overhead? That could reduce object counts by ~30% (less bookkeeping) but may increase internal waste. Do we have math on trade-off?
ashley: We simulated histogram of allocation sizes from traces; 60% of small allocations are 40–60B. Moving min -> 64B reduces split churn. We should run a canary with 64B min and compaction enabled.
samir: Also consider 'hot-slice' reusing: keep a per-thread hot cache of recently freed small blocks to avoid touching global slab free lists; that reduces contention and can decrease fragmentation by reuse locality.
nisha: Agreed. Action plan proposal: 1) Canary with min-block-size=64B + compactor disabled, compare memory curve; 2) Canary with min-block-size=64B + background compactor (budgeted); 3) If both look good, enable hot-slice reuse in allocator. Roll window 5% traffic, 30min run.
maria: I'll prepare the artifacts: repro script, pprof snapshot, and canary config. Attaching quick config snippet:
```yaml
kv_allocator:
  min_block_size: 64
  per_thread_hot_cache: 128
  compactor:
    enabled: true
    budget_ms_per_minute: 50
    target_fragmentation_ratio: 0.25
```
kevin: Also add a metric: kv.free_frag_ratio and kv.small_bucket_count so we can graph pre/post.
ashley: And add trace-tags so we can correlate batch-depth -> pin-time per-request.
compactor-bot: compaction-job scheduled: canary-kv-compact-493210 [start: 4932103000, shards: 6, budget: 50ms/min] :gear: 
maria: Thanks. I'll kick off the canary tomorrow morning and paste results in this thread. Initial priority: confirm whether this is a fragmentation accumulation (allocator behavior) vs. pinning due to batching.
kevin: If canary shows improvement, we should still run longer stress (6h) to ensure no slow creep.
ashley: Agreed. Also check disk-backed paging paths — if paging is happening under load it can amplify frag effects.
samir: Great. I'll draft a short RFC for a low-overhead incremental compactor and block-size trade matrix.
maria: Sweet. tagging @eng-runtime for visibility. :eyes:
